target_customer: Pet owners (dogs and cats) in US metros who want a vet to visit their home or workplace
problem: Taking a pet to a clinic is stressful and time consuming, and owners wanted veterinary care delivered at home.
business_model: Flat fee per house call with add-on charges for diagnostics and vaccines; vets paid a flat fee per visit
product_category: Veterinary house call marketplace and services

founders.name: Joe Waltman
previous_startups: Email marketing company sold to Twitter (with Soren Berg)
founders.background_notes: TechCrunch Jan 2015 states he and Berg previously sold an email marketing company to Twitter.

founders.name: Soren Berg
previous_startups: Email marketing company sold to Twitter (with Joe Waltman)

founders.name: Katherine van Ekert
founders.background_notes: Listed as founder on the YC page; no background found.

exit.reason: Vetted bought VetPronto in cash and equity for an undisclosed price. The buyer later shut down in Feb 2020 and a founder post said the sale was not a happy ending for shareholders.

competitors.name: BarkCare (Bark and Co.)
competitors.what: In-home vet service from a New York e-commerce startup
competitors.traction_then: TechCrunch said Bark had since deprioritized the service

technical_complexity.rationale: Scheduling, records, telemedicine and pharmacy integration were standard software work; the hard part was operations and recruiting vets.

defensibility.rationale: Services were copyable by any vet group, and an almost identical peer (Vetted) existed in Los Angeles.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Bark deprioritized its service, but a similar startup, Vetted, bought VetPronto in November 2017.

market_need_then: TechCrunch described owners paying 129 dollars per house call at launch, and coverage called the concept an Uber for vets even though vets were paid a flat 100 dollars per call.

branding.domain_note: vetpronto.com now redirects to a GoDaddy for sale page.
branding.community_and_virality: Local and trade press covered the launch (TechCrunch, Bernalwood, Tech.co) and a 2016 Wefunder campaign drew 636 small investors.

brand_strength.rationale: Local press and a crowd round show some awareness, but no source shows a distinctive visual identity or brand driven growth, and the acquirer planned to fold it under its own brand.

outcome_analysis: VetPronto launched house call vet visits in San Francisco in 2015 and expanded to seven metros but raised only about 1.3 million dollars in total. Founder accounts summarized by a directory say it never found a cost effective way to acquire pet owners and never won a professional lead investor, and vets earned a flat 100 dollars per visit against a 129 dollar price. Vetted bought it in November 2017 and then shut down in 2020, so shareholders and founders did not get a good outcome.
notes: The Wefunder round of 362,718 dollars from 636 investors is reported by Wefunder (search listing) and the HealthcareDiscovery profile; Bouncewatch lists a 365K seed dated Sept 2016 led by James Sowers, which likely refers to the same Form C raise. TechCrunch 2017 states about 1.3 million dollars raised in total, so about 0.8 million is unaccounted for by recorded rounds (a friends and family round is mentioned without amount). The post mortem reasons and the Vetted shutdown date come from the HealthcareDiscovery page quoting Joe Waltman posts on Medium, which could not be opened; Medium returned 403. Katherine van Ekert later dated the sale to 2020, conflicting with TechCrunch 2017. Brian Hur, a practicing vet, is named by TechCrunch as handling early appointments but is not called a co-founder, so he is not listed. The vetpronto.com site is for sale.
